stops.name: Trier, the house in the Brückergasse
stops.campa: At two in the morning of the fifth of May, in the baroque house at Brückergasse 664, a son is born to the advocate Heinrich Marx and Henriette née Presburg. Trier is the oldest city of Germany, Roman before Rome fell, and on both sides the child descends from unbroken lines of rabbis: his grandfather Meier Halevi was rabbi of this very town, his uncle holds the office still. The father has lately crossed to the Prussian church so that he may keep his practice at the bar. They name the boy Karl. The Moselle runs past the walls, patient as history.

stops.name: Trier, the parlour baptism in the Simeonstraße
stops.campa: In the family's rooms near the Porta Nigra, no church, no crowd, the military chaplain Mühlenhoff pours the water of Prussian Christianity over Karl, six years old, and over his brothers and sisters with him. The father went first, years ago; the mother, whose parents still live in the old faith in Nijmegen, will wait until her own father dies. So the grandson of the rabbis of Trier becomes, on paper, an Evangelical Christian, and keeps for life the double sight of the man baptized at home: inside every congregation, belonging to none.

stops.name: Trier, the walks with Baron von Westphalen
stops.campa: Ludwig von Westphalen, Prussian councillor, half a Scot by his mother's line of Argyll, takes the schoolboy walking through the vineyards and the Roman ruins above the Moselle. He recites Homer and whole scenes of Shakespeare from memory; he speaks of Saint-Simon and of the coming reign of association. Karl drinks it all. In the Baron's tall house he also finds the Baron's daughter Jenny, four years his elder, the most beautiful girl in Trier, the queen of its ballrooms. The old man is planting two loves at once: the Greeks, and her.
stops.quote: You, my fatherly friend, were always a living argumentum ad oculos to me, that idealism is no figment of the imagination, but a truth.
stops.quote_source: Dedication of his doctoral dissertation to Ludwig von Westphalen, 1841

stops.name: Trier, the Gymnasium and the examination essay
stops.campa: In the old Jesuit college that houses the Friedrich-Wilhelm-Gymnasium, the seventeen-year-old sits his leaving examinations under the liberal headmaster Wittenbach, whom the police already watch. For the German essay on the choice of a profession he writes a page that reads, afterwards, like a sealed prophecy: that a man cannot choose freely, that his relations in society have begun before he can determine them, and that the surest greatness belongs to the one who works for the whole. In October a boat carries him down the Moselle toward Bonn, and Trier keeps only his childhood.
stops.quote: The chief guide which must direct us in the choice of a profession is the welfare of mankind and our own perfection.
stops.quote_source: Abitur essay, 'Reflections of a Young Man on the Choice of a Profession', August 1835

stops.name: Bonn, matriculation at the university
stops.campa: Karl matriculates in the faculty of law in the yellow electoral palace on the Rhine, and immediately studies everything except law: nine courses, Greek mythology, Homer, art history, verse. He joins the Poets' Club, where the police keep a list of names, and the Trier Tavern Club, where they keep a tab; the Landsmannschaft of his home town soon makes him one of its presidents. His father writes anxious, loving letters about money and moderation. The boy answers with poems. The Rhine at Bonn is broad and bright and full of student songs, and he sings them.

stops.name: Bonn, the Karzer and the duel
stops.campa: The wild year ripens. In June the university locks him a night in the Karzer, the student prison, for drunkenness and nocturnal uproar: visitors climb in through the window with more wine, as the custom is. Then the aristocratic Corps Borussia, Prussians who make the plebeian Trier boys kiss the ground, provoke him once too often; Karl fights a sabre duel with one of them and carries away a cut above the left eye. His father, horrified, asks whether duelling is so interwoven with philosophy, and pulls him out of Bonn to sober Berlin.

stops.name: Trier, the secret betrothal to Jenny von Westphalen
stops.campa: Home for the vacation between Bonn and Berlin, the eighteen-year-old wins what the ballrooms of the Rhineland could not: Jenny von Westphalen, the baron's daughter, breaks with a promising lieutenant and pledges herself in secret to the advocate's son, four years her junior, penniless, Jewish-born, incandescent. Her family must not know yet; only his father is told, and keeps the secret like contraband. The engagement will last seven clandestine years and cost her battles against her own blood. From Berlin he will send her three volumes of poems, oceans of them, all fire.
stops.quote: I can assure you, without the slightest romanticism, that I am head over heels in love, and indeed in the most serious way. I have been engaged for more than seven years, and my fiancée has fought the fiercest battles for me.

stops.name: Berlin, the university on Unter den Linden
stops.campa: He matriculates in law at the university of Hegel, dead five years and reigning still. Savigny lectures him on jurisprudence, Eduard Gans on the rational march of history; the city itself, barracks and ministries and sand, is a workhouse compared with the Rhine. Karl reads until his health cracks: he attempts a philosophy of law in three hundred pages and burns it, writes poems to the absent Jenny, sleeps little. Berlin will hold him six years and turn the poet into a dialectician. He leaves love behind him in Trier and walks into the cold light of the concept.
stops.quote: There are moments in one's life which are like frontier posts marking the completion of a period but at the same time clearly indicating a new direction.

stops.name: Stralau, the fishing village and the conversion to Hegel
stops.campa: Broken by overwork, the doctor orders him out of the city, and Karl lodges in the fishing village of Stralau on its green spit between the Spree and the Rummelsburg lake. Walking the shore to Berlin and back, lungs filling, he wrestles the philosophy he had meant to despise. He has read fragments of Hegel and disliked its grotesque craggy melody; now, in convalescence, he reads it end to end, and the enemy takes the fortress from within. He returns to town a Hegelian, chained, as he writes, to the ship like a lover to his mistress.
stops.quote: A curtain had fallen, my holy of holies was rent asunder, and new gods had to be installed... I arrived at the point of seeking the idea in the real itself.

stops.name: Berlin, the Doctors' Club and the doctorate of Prometheus
stops.campa: In Hippel's wine-cellar on the Friedrichstraße the Young Hegelians hold their symposium: Bruno Bauer, Köppen, Rutenberg; and the youngest of the Doctors' Club out-argues the doctors. His father has died; Prussia's new king is hounding Hegel's left-hand children out of every chair. Karl writes his dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, the physics of falling atoms and the swerve of freedom, and prefixes to it a hymn to the fire-thief. The University of Jena, sight unseen, sends him the doctor's diploma on the fifteenth of April. No German lectern will ever hold him.
stops.quote: Prometheus is the most eminent saint and martyr in the philosophical calendar.

stops.name: Cologne, the Rheinische Zeitung and the freedom of the press
stops.campa: Rhenish merchants and bankers have founded a liberal paper in Cologne, and from Trier and Bonn the young doctor begins to feed it thunder. His first great series, running from his twenty-fourth birthday, defends the freedom of the press against the Rhine Province Assembly with a wit the censors cannot quite catch in their nets. Readers ask who the anonymous Rhinelander is. The paper's circulation climbs. Cologne, cathedral crane frozen over the roofs, steamers on the river, money and Catholicism, becomes the arena where German philosophy first walks out of the seminar and into the street.
stops.quote: The free press is the ubiquitous vigilant eye of a people's soul, the embodiment of a people's faith in itself.
stops.quote_source: Rheinische Zeitung, debates on freedom of the press, May 1842

stops.name: Cologne: editor-in-chief, and the theft of wood
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of October Marx takes the editor's chair, and the moderate sheet becomes the most dangerous paper in Prussia; within months its circulation triples. He writes on the law against the gathering of fallen wood, by which the poor of the Moselle are made criminals for the customary rights of centuries, and on the misery of the wine-growers of his home valley. Here, he will say ever after, the philosopher first stubbed his toe on economics. In November a cool young Englishman-from-Barmen named Engels calls at the office; the editor receives him with reserve.
stops.quote: In the year 1842-43, as editor of the Rheinische Zeitung, I first found myself in the embarrassing position of having to discuss what is known as material interests.
stops.quote_source: Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859
